 K-drama writers discuss global storytelling, challenges
 Students flocked to Tutor Campus Center on Thursday to hear acclaimed writers speak on their respective successes.
 By ANNE TILLEY
 October 26, 2026 
 Panelists shared components of their respective Korean drama series that allowed them to make it big in global markets. (Anne Tilley / Daily Trojan) 
 Dramatic Korean scripted television series, or K-dramas, have exploded onto the global cultural stage in the past decade, transcending language barriers and finding a massive audience in the West, particularly in North America.  
 The unprecedented success of “Squid Game” in 2021, which became the first Korean series to top the charts of Netflix, is often cited as a catalyst for an influx of more recent series, paving the way for writers and executives to gamble on a genre previously viewed as only regionally successful.  
 Thursday’s conversation, moderated by Hye Jin Lee, a clinical associate professor of communication, and hosted along with the Korean Creative Content Agency and the Korean Consulate. Oh Sang-ho and Shin Yoo-dam — writers of “Taxi Driver” and “Marry My Husband,” respectively — discussed their groundbreaking successes.

 The panel also considered the adversities they faced. For Oh, his main writing challenge was “How do we structure the story to make it attractive to a global audience?” 
 “Taxi Driver,” a crime action thriller series, follows an unassuming taxi driver who enacts revenge on behalf of his passengers who cannot seek it themselves. Oh said the series is heavily inspired by his perspective on societal imbalances.  
 “As a writer, when you’re writing about things, you cannot help but include things you’re really frustrated about [in] the world, or what you want to change,” Oh said. “I really had a lot of thoughts about the fact that the world is not just.”  
 Oh described how this lens emotionally fueled his vigilante justice story, forcing him to deviate from his typical writing process. Whereas many narratives revolve around characters wanting something they cannot have, Oh worried the series would lose viewers if it were simply paralleling audiences’ own daily grievances, as it was thematically grounded in harrowing realities.  
 In order to prevent any of this disengagement, he added a subtle device surrounding protagonist Kim Do-gi (Lee Je-hoon), who audiences never see be physically harmed by another character.  
 “If you see the main character, he isn’t hit at all. He just hits other people,” Oh said. “I don’t give the main characters a lot of strife to go through.”  
 Shin’s “Marry My Husband” follows a similar concept of revenge, although in vastly different circumstances: Her central protagonist, Kang Ji-Won (Park Min-young), goes back in time after being killed by her husband in order to alter her fate.  
 Ji-Won’s revenge comes in the form of resolving everyday conflicts, instead of having a clear antagonist — similar to the external conflict of an “unjust world” in “Taxi Driver” — which served as a difficult challenge for Song when pitching to executives.  
 “Instead of avenging parents or partners, this was more so avenging everyday pet peeves or things that can irk you in daily life,” Shin said. “It’s really fun.” 
 Both writers also attributed the global success of their K-dramas to the universal emotions they appeal to. Shin said the romantic plots in “Marry My Husband” are evident across cultures, not confined by regional or national restrictions, as “everybody is interested in dating all around the world.”   
 Similarly, Oh’s cry against the unfair is applicable to all who face injustice in their own everyday lives, luring in viewers across language and societal barriers.  
 “I guess I have a lot of qualms with society,” Oh said. 
 The panel provided an insightful opportunity for students interested in both the entertainment industry and fans of the K-drama genre, including Sally Xie, a sophomore majoring in public relations and advertising. 
 “K-dram as have really risen, … especially coming onto Netflix and [in] the North [American] audience,” Xie said. “I feel like K-dramas have their own style.”   
 Irena Zhang, a sophomore majoring in communication, shared similar sentiments regarding the panel’s fun yet informative conversations, particularly regarding the writers’ anecdotes regarding the creation of their dramas. 
 “It’s pretty fun to know about their thoughts behind it,” Zhang said.  
 Despite their success, both writers continue to push forward, seeking to further the deviation from traditional narrative arcs, continue telling stories that attract varying audiences and push beyond what is deemed possible in their distinct genres.  
 When describing her upcoming projects, Shin said she is striving to “tell the most widespread, relatable stories that deal with the most specific situations,” resuming her globalization of emotional storytelling.  
 Oh similarly cited the rapid rise of K-dramas in popularity as a further incentive, spurring him to continue to write bold, inventive stories.  
 “Because of production limitations, usually I do limit myself on what I imagine based on what is able to be filmed,” Oh said. “[But as] people around the world have started to really watch Korean content, I’ve gained the confidence to be able to imagine more broadly and widely.”
